<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and the AI Literacy Guide by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was 1.0 point higher (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered and mostly indistinguishable from zero. With 44 uncorrected tests, small arms and p-values near 0.05, the isolated effects should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy gain across all 11 arms was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, one-sided); AI Literacy Guide raised it by 4.7 points (95% CI [+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: dropping attention-check failures reportedly removed the two accuracy gains, but this check is unreviewed model code.
- Caveat: 44 arm-level tests with no multiplicity correction, several small arms, and most p-values near 0.05, so isolated effects are fragile.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The plan was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, registered 2023-11-15, amending #151208). Some data existed at registration, but the last two batches followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 were analysed; the control group is the comparison for all 11 arms. Arm sizes range from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). Rows with missing outcome values were dropped model by model, usually a handful per arm. Accuracy is a proportion correct, reported here in percentage points.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=total_score -->
### H1. Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly)

*Each intervention changes AI-detection accuracy relative to control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Two interventions raised total accuracy relative to control (69.3% correct). Automated Flagging was 4.4 points higher (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004) and the AI Literacy Guide 4.7 points higher (95% CI [0.2, 9.2], p=0.043). ### E1. H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures

Respondents who fail both knowledge questions may not have engaged with the task, so excluding them tests whether registered H1 effects are driven by inattentive respondents. Re-fit the registered H1 model (total_score ~ arm × covariates, IPW, HC2) on the subsample with pk_score >= 1 (n=1417 vs 2030 full); compare arm-level ATEs and SEs side by side.

**Finding.** Excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2030→1417) eliminated the two nominally significant registered effects (Automated Flagging p=0.004→ns; AI Literacy Guide p=0.043→ns), suggesting those effects were concentrated among respondents who also passed the knowledge checks.

![H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures](figures/E1_h1_no_attention_fail.png)

Unreviewed model code reports that excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2,030 to 1,417) left the two accuracy gains nonsignificant. This disagrees with the registered H1 estimates, which used the full sample; the check has not been reviewed.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

Prior findings offer partial, indirect support for the study's hypotheses. Lewandowsky and van der Linden (2021) document that inoculation and prebunking interventions can shift attitudes toward misinformation, providing a basis for expecting effects on attitudes (H2) and trust in online information (H4). Ecker et al. (2022) identify psychological drivers that make misinformation beliefs resistant to correction, suggesting that attitude and trust outcomes may be harder to move than detection accuracy (H1). Capraro et al. (2024) frame generative AI as a new vector for (mis)information, contextualizing why detection of AI-generated posts (H5) and recognition of authentic posts (H6) are relevant outcomes. The retrieved list is thin on work directly addressing human detection of AI-generated text specifically; most supporting evidence is about misinformation more broadly.

A live disagreement concerns the sufficiency of individual-level interventions. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level behavioral solutions has led policy astray and that system-level changes are necessary, which contests the premise that the study's individual-level design can produce meaningful effects on any of its outcomes. Ecker et al. (2022) reinforce this skepticism by showing that belief correction is psychologically difficult. The study's controlled intervention design can speak to whether individual-level changes in detection accuracy, confidence, attitudes, or trust are detectable at all, but it cannot adjudicate the broader claim that such changes are insufficient without system-level reform.

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

The registered hypotheses involve 44 arm-level tests across four outcomes with no multiplicity correction, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The accuracy gains are modest and sit near the threshold for the AI Literacy Guide. Some data were collected before registration. The sample is an online US panel, and the unreviewed attention-check analysis suggests results may depend on respondent attentiveness. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (detecting AI posts, recognising authentic posts) were not registered and are post hoc.

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished survey experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures.

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

## Exploratory
- E1: H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures — Excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2030→1417) eliminated the two nominally significant registered effects (Automated Flagging p=0.004→ns; AI Literacy Guide p=0.043→ns), suggesting those effects were concentrated among respondents who also passed the knowledge checks. ## Literature note
Prior findings offer partial, indirect support for the study's hypotheses. Lewandowsky and van der Linden (2021) document that inoculation and prebunking interventions can shift attitudes toward misinformation, providing a basis for expecting effects on attitudes (H2) and trust in online information (H4). Ecker et al. (2022) identify psychological drivers that make misinformation beliefs resistant to correction, suggesting that attitude and trust outcomes may be harder to move than detection accuracy (H1). Capraro et al. (2024) frame generative AI as a new vector for (mis)information, contextualizing why detection of AI-generated posts (H5) and recognition of authentic posts (H6) are relevant outcomes. The retrieved list is thin on work directly addressing human detection of AI-generated text specifically; most supporting evidence is about misinformation more broadly.

A live disagreement concerns the sufficiency of individual-level interventions. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level behavioral solutions has led policy astray and that system-level changes are necessary, which contests the premise that the study's individual-level design can produce meaningful effects on any of its outcomes. Ecker et al. (2022) reinforce this skepticism by showing that belief correction is psychologically difficult. The study's controlled intervention design can speak to whether individual-level changes in detection accuracy, confidence, attitudes, or trust are detectable at all, but it cannot adjudicate the broader claim that such changes are insufficient without system-level reform.

## Revised report
# Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

*Yamil Velez · 2026-10-03 · N = 2,030 analysed of 2,257 collected · survey experiment*

![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: major revision](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #151,281](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: survey experiment](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

[Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/ai-discernment

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The plan was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15, amending #151208). Some data existed at registration; batches 3-4 followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 were analysed; the control group is the comparison for all 11 arms. Arm sizes range from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). Rows with missing outcome values were dropped model by model, usually a handful per arm. Models use inverse-probability weights (1 / pr); their construction, the exclusion rules behind the 227 dropped respondents and attrition by arm are not documented in the materials supplied here, and differential attrition was not checked.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=total_score -->
### H1. Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly)

*Each intervention changes AI-detection accuracy relative to control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Two interventions raised total accuracy relative to control (69.3% correct). Automated Flagging was 4.4 points higher (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004) and the AI Literacy Guide about 4.7 points higher, a borderline gain whose CI barely excludes zero (95% CI [0.2, 9.2], p=0.043). Mindfulness was 3.9 points lower (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3], p=0.032). P-values are two-sided. The other eight arms were within about ±2 points of control and not distinguishable from it. ### E1. H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures

Respondents who fail both knowledge questions may not have engaged with the task, so excluding them tests whether registered H1 effects are driven by inattentive respondents. Re-fit the registered H1 model (total_score ~ arm × covariates, IPW, HC2) on the subsample with pk_score >= 1 (n=1417 vs 2030 full); compare arm-level ATEs and SEs side by side.

**Finding.** Excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2030→1417) eliminated the two nominally significant registered effects (Automated Flagging p=0.004→ns; AI Literacy Guide p=0.043→ns), suggesting those effects were concentrated among respondents who also passed the knowledge checks.

Unreviewed model code reports that a low-knowledge exclusion (pk_score below 1, n 2,030 to 1,417; not a true attention check) removed the two accuracy gains. The output table is empty, so this cannot be verified and is not used to qualify the registered H1 estimates.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

Prior findings offer partial, indirect support for the study's hypotheses. Lewandowsky and van der Linden (2021) document that inoculation and prebunking interventions can shift attitudes toward misinformation, providing a basis for expecting effects on attitudes (H2) and trust in online information (H4). Ecker et al. (2022) identify psychological drivers that make misinformation beliefs resistant to correction, suggesting that attitude and trust outcomes may be harder to move than detection accuracy (H1). Capraro et al. (2024) frame generative AI as a new vector for (mis)information, contextualizing why detection of AI-generated posts (H5) and recognition of authentic posts (H6) are relevant outcomes. The retrieved list is thin on work directly addressing human detection of AI-generated text specifically; most supporting evidence is about misinformation more broadly.

A live disagreement concerns the sufficiency of individual-level interventions. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level behavioral solutions has led policy astray and that system-level changes are necessary, which contests the premise that the study's individual-level design can produce meaningful effects on any of its outcomes. Ecker et al. (2022) reinforce this skepticism by showing that belief correction is psychologically difficult. The study's controlled intervention design can speak to whether individual-level changes in detection accuracy, confidence, attitudes, or trust are detectable at all, but it cannot adjudicate the broader claim that such changes are insufficient without system-level reform.

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Report
# Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

*Yamil Velez · 2026-10-03 · N = 2,030 analysed of 2,257 collected · survey experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: major revision](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #151,281](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: survey experiment](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

Reviewer pass: yes. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. (2026). Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media? [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/ai-discernment

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The plan was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15, amending #151208). Some data existed at registration; batches 3-4 followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 were analysed; the control group is the comparison for all 11 arms. Arm sizes range from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). Rows with missing outcome values were dropped model by model, usually a handful per arm. Models use inverse-probability weights (1 / pr); their construction, the exclusion rules behind the 227 dropped respondents and attrition by arm are not documented in the materials supplied here, and differential attrition was not checked.

*Pre-registered.*

### E1. H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures

Respondents who fail both knowledge questions may not have engaged with the task, so excluding them tests whether registered H1 effects are driven by inattentive respondents. Re-fit the registered H1 model (total_score ~ arm × covariates, IPW, HC2) on the subsample with pk_score >= 1 (n=1417 vs 2030 full); compare arm-level ATEs and SEs side by side.

**Finding.** Excluding 613 attention-check failures (n 2030→1417) eliminated the two nominally significant registered effects (Automated Flagging p=0.004→ns; AI Literacy Guide p=0.043→ns), suggesting those effects were concentrated among respondents who also passed the knowledge checks.

![H1 robustness: excluding attention-check failures](figures/E1_h1_no_attention_fail.png)

Unreviewed model code reports that a low-knowledge exclusion (pk_score below 1, n 2,030 to 1,417; not a true attention check) removed the two accuracy gains. The output table is empty, so this cannot be verified and is not used to qualify the registered H1 estimates.

### E2. H1 heterogeneity by prior AI familiarity

Interventions that teach AI detection may work differently for respondents who already know AI tools versus those who do not; this checks whether registered H1 effects are concentrated among low-familiarity respondents. Split sample at the median of ai_scale (0.143); re-fit the registered H1 model separately in each half; compare arm-level ATEs.

**Finding.** No arm reached p<0.05 in either the low-familiarity or high-familiarity subsample, indicating the registered H1 effects (Automated Flagging, AI Literacy Guide) are not concentrated in either familiarity group and likely reflect sampling variability.

![H1 heterogeneity by prior AI familiarity](figures/E2_h1_ai_familiarity.png)

An unreviewed split by prior AI familiarity has an empty output table and no interaction test. Subgroups are small, so it is inconclusive whether the accuracy effects differ by familiarity.

### E3. Placebo: effect of interventions on pre-treatment knowledge (pk_score)

If interventions affect a pre-treatment knowledge score, this would indicate a manipulation or implementation problem; a null result supports the validity of the experimental design. Weighted least squares (IPW, HC2) of pk_score on arm dummies for all 11 treatment arms vs control (n=2030).

**Finding.** No intervention significantly affected pre-treatment knowledge (all p > 0.116, max p = 0.816), confirming the randomisation and that no arm differentially exposed respondents to the knowledge questions.

An unreviewed placebo check on pk_score found no arm clearly differing from control (min p=0.116, max 0.816), consistent with balance. Its timing relative to treatment is unclear and no joint F-test is reported, so it does not confirm randomisation.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

Prior findings offer partial, indirect support for the study's hypotheses. Lewandowsky and van der Linden (2021) document that inoculation and prebunking interventions can shift attitudes toward misinformation, providing a basis for expecting effects on attitudes (H2) and trust in online information (H4). Ecker et al. (2022) identify psychological drivers that make misinformation beliefs resistant to correction, suggesting that attitude and trust outcomes may be harder to move than detection accuracy (H1). Capraro et al. (2024) frame generative AI as a new vector for (mis)information, contextualizing why detection of AI-generated posts (H5) and recognition of authentic posts (H6) are relevant outcomes. The retrieved list is thin on work directly addressing human detection of AI-generated text specifically; most supporting evidence is about misinformation more broadly.

A live disagreement concerns the sufficiency of individual-level interventions. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level behavioral solutions has led policy astray and that system-level changes are necessary, which contests the premise that the study's individual-level design can produce meaningful effects on any of its outcomes. Ecker et al. (2022) reinforce this skepticism by showing that belief correction is psychologically difficult. The study's controlled intervention design can speak to whether individual-level changes in detection accuracy, confidence, attitudes, or trust are detectable at all, but it cannot adjudicate the broader claim that such changes are insufficient without system-level reform.

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Editor's unresolved questions
- U1: Do the interventions improve true discernment between AI-generated and authentic media, or do they shift response bias towards labelling items as AI? - U2: Do the Automated Flagging and AI Literacy Guide gains replicate in a preregistered, adequately powered sample with a multiplicity plan? (why this study cannot settle it: These effects are nominal (p=0.004 and p=0.043) in uncorrected tests with small arms, and the exploratory exclusion check is unreliable as reported.)

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Signal-detection replication of labels and literacy guide
Question: Do Automated Flagging and the AI Literacy Guide raise sensitivity (d') to AI-generated media, or only shift the criterion?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the measurement failure: collects item-level real/AI judgments plus a confidence rating so d' and criterion can be estimated (U1), and gives a clean replication of the two nominal effects (U2).
Design sketch: Three arms: control, automated-detector label, literacy guide. Each respondent judges 40 items, half AI and half authentic, with item-level responses and a 1-6 confidence scale. Each item is randomly flagged or unflagged for a within-subject element. Outcome: d' and criterion c, estimated from a multilevel signal-detection model. US online panel, with exclusion rules and a multiplicity plan registered in advance.
Power target: about 420 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (H1 observed 0.044 (Automated Flagging) shrunk toward the 0.03 MDE of the largest arm (0.0318 at n=333); a 3-point gain at 80% power needs roughly 420 per arm.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Can individual-level interventions meaningfully improve resistance to misinformation?): (a) Prebunking, inoculation and literacy tools shift belief and detection, so individual-level interventions are worthwhile. versus (b) Individual-level fixes are small and fragile, and system-level change is needed.. The source study says: Leans toward b: the pooled accuracy effect is 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), and only labels from an automated detector showed a possibly real gain. The study cannot rule out small effects or speak to system-level reform.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1, U2

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

Limitations: No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Do the interventions improve true discernment between AI-generated and authentic media, or do they shift response bias towards labelling items as AI? (why this study cannot settle it: The data contain only share-correct scores for fake and real posts, with no per-item responses. This study cannot cleanly separate sensitivity from bias.)
- U2: Do the Automated Flagging and AI Literacy Guide gains replicate in a preregistered, adequately powered sample with a multiplicity plan? (why this study cannot settle it: These effects are nominal (p=0.004 and p=0.043) in uncorrected tests with small arms, and the exploratory exclusion check is unreliable as reported.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Change 'one-sided' to two-sided in Key findings.
- Populate the E1 and E2 tables or remove their conclusions, relabel E1 as a low-knowledge exclusion, and soften E2 to inconclusive.
- State that no multiplicity correction was registered, that 44 tests were run, and that the isolated effects are nominal.
- Add the H5 prose, write p<0.001 instead of p=0.000, and discuss the response-bias reading of H5 against H6.
- Report exclusion rules, IPW construction and attrition by arm, and note that some data pre-dated registration.
- Clean the related-work list (remove the kidney disease, PRISMA-P and mortality references) and correct the E3 wording.

design.title: Signal-detection replication of labels and literacy guide
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to control, automated-detector label, or AI literacy guide. They then judge 40 images (20 AI, 20 authentic), giving real/AI judgments and 1-6 confidence for each. In the label arm and the other arms alike, each item is randomly shown with or without a detector flag, except that the flag is only displayed in the label arm.
design.hypothesis: Automated labels and the literacy guide raise d' relative to control; if the effects are only criterion shifts, d' will not differ and c will move toward more AI responses.
design.primaryOutcome: Sensitivity d' and criterion c from a multilevel signal-detection model (probit mixed model of AI judgment on true item status, arm, and their interaction, with random effects for respondent and item).
design.comparison: Each treatment arm versus control on d' and c; Holm correction across the two primary d' contrasts; criterion contrasts secondary; within-arm flagged versus unflagged items exploratory.
design.population: US adults from an online panel, about 420 per arm (1,260 total), with preregistered exclusions for failed attention check, speeding, and duplicate responses.

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

Limitations: No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Do the interventions improve true discernment between AI-generated and authentic media, or do they shift response bias towards labelling items as AI? (why this study cannot settle it: The data contain only share-correct scores for fake and real posts, with no per-item responses. This study cannot cleanly separate sensitivity from bias.)
- U2: Do the Automated Flagging and AI Literacy Guide gains replicate in a preregistered, adequately powered sample with a multiplicity plan? (why this study cannot settle it: These effects are nominal (p=0.004 and p=0.043) in uncorrected tests with small arms, and the exploratory exclusion check is unreliable as reported.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Change 'one-sided' to two-sided in Key findings.
- Populate the E1 and E2 tables or remove their conclusions, relabel E1 as a low-knowledge exclusion, and soften E2 to inconclusive.
- State that no multiplicity correction was registered, that 44 tests were run, and that the isolated effects are nominal.
- Add the H5 prose, write p<0.001 instead of p=0.000, and discuss the response-bias reading of H5 against H6.
- Report exclusion rules, IPW construction and attrition by arm, and note that some data pre-dated registration.
- Clean the related-work list (remove the kidney disease, PRISMA-P and mortality references) and correct the E3 wording.

function.name: record_result

value.title: Does label benefit depend on stimulus difficulty and AI familiarity?
value.rationale: Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (p=0.004) in the source study, but the familiarity heterogeneity table (E2) was empty and some high-familiarity arm halves had n=38 or fewer. This follow-up tests whether the gain holds across easy vs hard stimuli and across prior AI familiarity, with enough power for an interaction test.
value.contribution: Tests whether the automated-label gain is conditional on stimulus difficulty and prior AI familiarity, using a preregistered moderator and an adequately powered sample.
limitations: Interaction tests need several hundred respondents per cell, so the interaction may remain underpowered.
Oversampling high-familiarity respondents may limit generalisation to the whole population.
Generator age is only a proxy for difficulty.

design.title: Automated labels by stimulus difficulty and AI familiarity
design.overview: Respondents first report AI familiarity (ai_scale), with high-familiarity respondents oversampled. They are then randomised to a control or an automated AI-detection label. Each respondent judges 8 posts (images and text) in a within-person mix of older-generator (easy) and recent-generator (hard) AI outputs and authentic items. The outcome is d' and its interaction with difficulty and with familiarity.
design.hypothesis: H1: automated labels raise d' relative to control (0.035 minimum effect). H2: the label gain is smaller for hard (recent-generator) stimuli. H3: the label gain differs by ai_scale (high vs low familiarity).
design.primaryOutcome: Discernment d' (z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate)) across the 8 posts, with condition by difficulty and condition by ai_scale interaction tests.
design.comparison: Control vs automated label, crossed within person with stimulus difficulty (older vs recent generator), and moderated by ai_scale (pre-treatment).
design.population: US online panel adults, with high AI-familiarity respondents oversampled.

d' is computed per respondent with a log-linear correction; a multiplicity plan (Holm across H1-H3) is preregistered.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
Question: Are the H5 gains from Breathing, Nudge and Guide a bias toward answering AI, or better discernment?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Discriminates the two positions of D1 by separating bias from sensitivity. If interventions work, d' rises under any base rate. If the effects are bias, they vanish or flip when the share of AI items changes.
Design sketch: 2x3 design: feed with 20% or 80% AI items, crossed with control, Breathing and Guide. Item-level responses; outcome d' and criterion, with an interaction test of intervention by base rate. A payoff-for-accuracy variant can be added as a robustness check.
Power target: about 300 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (H5 observed 0.066-0.091 with SE about 0.03; 300 per cell detects 0.04-0.05 at 80% power.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Can individual-level interventions meaningfully improve resistance to misinformation?): (a) Prebunking, inoculation and literacy tools shift belief and detection, so individual-level interventions are worthwhile. versus (b) Individual-level fixes are small and fragile, and system-level change is needed.. The source study says: Leans toward b: the pooled accuracy effect is 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), and only labels from an automated detector showed a possibly real gain. The study cannot rule out small effects or speak to system-level reform.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

Limitations: No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Do the interventions improve true discernment between AI-generated and authentic media, or do they shift response bias towards labelling items as AI? (why this study cannot settle it: The data contain only share-correct scores for fake and real posts, with no per-item responses. This study cannot cleanly separate sensitivity from bias.)
- U2: Do the Automated Flagging and AI Literacy Guide gains replicate in a preregistered, adequately powered sample with a multiplicity plan? (why this study cannot settle it: These effects are nominal (p=0.004 and p=0.043) in uncorrected tests with small arms, and the exploratory exclusion check is unreliable as reported.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Change 'one-sided' to two-sided in Key findings.
- Populate the E1 and E2 tables or remove their conclusions, relabel E1 as a low-knowledge exclusion, and soften E2 to inconclusive.
- State that no multiplicity correction was registered, that 44 tests were run, and that the isolated effects are nominal.
- Add the H5 prose, write p<0.001 instead of p=0.000, and discuss the response-bias reading of H5 against H6.
- Report exclusion rules, IPW construction and attrition by arm, and note that some data pre-dated registration.
- Clean the related-work list (remove the kidney disease, PRISMA-P and mortality references) and correct the E3 wording.

design.title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to a feed with 20% or 80% AI items and, independently, to control, Breathing Exercise or AI Literacy Guide. They judge each of 20 items as AI-generated or authentic. Item-level responses give d' and criterion c per person.
design.hypothesis: If the interventions improve discernment, d' rises relative to control at both base rates and the intervention by base-rate interaction on d' is near zero. If they only bias responses toward answering AI, d' does not differ and c shifts toward AI responses, and this shift shrinks or reverses when 80% of items are AI.
design.primaryOutcome: Signal-detection sensitivity d' per respondent, with criterion c as co-primary, computed from 20 item-level AI/authentic judgments.
design.comparison: Breathing and Guide vs control on d' and c, within each base rate. Interaction test of intervention by base rate. Optional accuracy-payoff robustness check.
design.population: US online panel adults, as in the source study.

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
Question: Are the H5 gains from Breathing, Nudge and Guide a bias toward answering AI, or better discernment?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Discriminates the two positions of D1 by separating bias from sensitivity. If interventions work, d' rises under any base rate. If the effects are bias, they vanish or flip when the share of AI items changes.
Design sketch: 2x3 design: feed with 20% or 80% AI items, crossed with control, Breathing and Guide. Item-level responses; outcome d' and criterion, with an interaction test of intervention by base rate. A payoff-for-accuracy variant can be added as a robustness check.
Power target: about 300 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (H5 observed 0.066-0.091 with SE about 0.03; 300 per cell detects 0.04-0.05 at 80% power.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Can individual-level interventions meaningfully improve resistance to misinformation?): (a) Prebunking, inoculation and literacy tools shift belief and detection, so individual-level interventions are worthwhile. versus (b) Individual-level fixes are small and fragile, and system-level change is needed.. The source study says: Leans toward b: the pooled accuracy effect is 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), and only labels from an automated detector showed a possibly real gain. The study cannot rule out small effects or speak to system-level reform.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can misinformation-style interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with a US panel (fielded October 30 to November 21, 2023), randomising respondents to a control or one of 11 interventions, including flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, nudges, mindfulness and breathing exercises, inoculation, and AI literacy materials. Of 2,257 respondents, 2,030 were analysed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide showed a borderline gain of about 4.7 points, with a CI barely excluding zero ([0.2, 9.2]). Mindfulness lowered accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). Pooled across arms, accuracy was about 1 point higher, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, 2.4]). Effects on attitudes, confidence and trust were scattered. No multiplicity correction was registered across 44 tests, so isolated effects are nominal and should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most interventions did not measurably improve people's accuracy in spotting AI-generated media; the pooled accuracy difference across all 11 arms was about 1 point, not distinguishable from zero (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Registered: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [+1.4, +7.3], p=0.004, two-sided); the AI Literacy Guide gain of 4.7 points had a CI barely excluding zero ([+0.2, +9.2]).
- Registered: Mindfulness lowered total accuracy by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]); AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection by 0.69 scale points (95% CI [−1.20, −0.17]).
- Exploratory: Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge were associated with higher detection of AI-generated posts, but recognition of authentic posts did not rise alongside, which fits a response-bias reading.
- Caveat: 44 tests were run with no registered multiplicity correction, several arms are small, and isolated effects are nominal and fragile.

Limitations: No multiplicity correction was registered, and 44 registered arm-level tests were run, so a few nominal results at p between 0.01 and 0.05 would be expected by chance; the isolated effects are nominal. Several arms are small (Inoculation n=78, AI Literacy Infographic 2 n=80), giving wide intervals. The AI Literacy Guide gain sits near the threshold. Some data were collected before registration. Exclusion rules, weight construction and attrition by arm are not documented. The sample is an online US panel. Confidence, attitude and trust effects are scattered rather than consistent. Exploratory outcomes (H5, H6) were not registered and are post hoc.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Do the interventions improve true discernment between AI-generated and authentic media, or do they shift response bias towards labelling items as AI? (why this study cannot settle it: The data contain only share-correct scores for fake and real posts, with no per-item responses. This study cannot cleanly separate sensitivity from bias.)
- U2: Do the Automated Flagging and AI Literacy Guide gains replicate in a preregistered, adequately powered sample with a multiplicity plan? (why this study cannot settle it: These effects are nominal (p=0.004 and p=0.043) in uncorrected tests with small arms, and the exploratory exclusion check is unreliable as reported.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Change 'one-sided' to two-sided in Key findings.
- Populate the E1 and E2 tables or remove their conclusions, relabel E1 as a low-knowledge exclusion, and soften E2 to inconclusive.
- State that no multiplicity correction was registered, that 44 tests were run, and that the isolated effects are nominal.
- Add the H5 prose, write p<0.001 instead of p=0.000, and discuss the response-bias reading of H5 against H6.
- Report exclusion rules, IPW construction and attrition by arm, and note that some data pre-dated registration.
- Clean the related-work list (remove the kidney disease, PRISMA-P and mortality references) and correct the E3 wording.

value.title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
value.rationale: The source found Breathing and Nudge raised detection of AI posts without raising recognition of authentic posts (H5 gains 0.066-0.091, SE about 0.03), which fits a bias toward answering AI. Pooled accuracy was only about 1 point (CI -0.3 to 2.4), so it is unclear whether individual interventions help. Changing the share of AI items separates a real sensitivity gain from a shifted answering criterion.
value.contribution: Tests whether intervention gains persist as d' under both 20% and 80% AI base rates, or vanish or flip as a criterion shift.
limitations: Base-rate manipulation may change participants' expectations and strategy, not just the criterion.
Feed items differ from the source's 24-item mix, so effects may not carry over directly.
Control, Breathing and Guide only; Nudge and Automated Flagging are not tested.
Online US panel; short exposure to each intervention.

design.title: Discernment vs response bias: manipulating base rates
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to a feed with 20% or 80% AI items and, independently, to control, Breathing Exercise or AI Literacy Guide. They judge each of 20 items as AI-generated or authentic. Item-level responses give d' and criterion c per person.
design.hypothesis: If the interventions improve discernment, d' rises relative to control at both base rates and the intervention by base-rate interaction on d' is near zero. If they only bias responses toward answering AI, d' does not differ and c shifts toward AI responses, and this shift shrinks or reverses when 80% of items are AI.
design.primaryOutcome: Signal-detection sensitivity d' per respondent, with criterion c as co-primary, computed from 20 item-level AI/authentic judgments.
design.comparison: Breathing and Guide vs control on d' and c, within each base rate. Interaction test of intervention by base rate. Optional accuracy-payoff robustness check.
design.population: US online panel adults, as in the source study.

questions.text: This is a research study about judging online media. Participation is voluntary and anonymous, and you may stop at any time. Do you agree to participate?
Have you ever interacted with any of the following tools?
Please do this box-breathing exercise for one minute: breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat calmly.

Guide: How to spot AI-generated media. Look for odd hands and teeth, warped text, inconsistent lighting and shadows, overly smooth skin, and unnatural motion or audio sync in videos. Examples of each artifact are shown. {{ed:guide_img}}
You will see 20 posts. For each, mark whether it is AI-generated or authentic. Go with your gut if unsure.
{{ed:item1}}
Is this post AI-generated or authentic?
{{ed:item2}}
Is this post AI-generated or authentic?
Please indicate your agreement.

rows.text: I feel confident in my ability to detect artificial intelligence.
I guessed AI more often than I guessed authentic.

questions.text: Thank you. Some posts were AI-generated and some authentic, and the share of each varied between participants. Your score does not affect your payment. The study examines whether tips and exercises improve real detection or just make people say AI more often.
